source: Free-Body Diagrams
Draw every force on one object as an arrow from its center, naming what exerts it.
Students draw a "force of motion" in the direction an object moves, or include forces the object exerts on other things.
You've met forces in Newton's Third Law and Friction. Before using Newton's laws on any problem, physicists draw a free-body diagram: one object, alone, with every force on it drawn as an arrow.

Draw the object as a box or a dot. For every force on it, draw an arrow from its center in the force's direction and name the object that exerts it. Contact forces come from things touching it; gravity comes from Earth.

Newton's laws relate the forces on one object to that object's motion. A diagram that leaves out a force, or adds one that isn't real, gives the wrong net force. Naming who exerts each force is the test: "the floor pushes up" is a real force; "the motion pushes forward" has no one doing the pushing, so it isn't a force.
Build the diagram: add each force from the list, drag its tip to set its size and direction, and check.
Worked examples
You push a box across a rough floor at a steady speed. What forces act on it?
A box pushed across a floor
Gravity, normal force, friction and your push
Earth: gravity, down. The floor: a normal force, up, and kinetic friction, opposite to the sliding.
Your hand: the push, along its direction.
Four forces. At steady speed the push balances friction and the normal force balances gravity.
A ball flies up and to the right after you throw it. Ignoring air, what forces act on it?
A ball in flight
Only gravity
Nothing touches it, so there are no contact forces.
Only Earth's gravity, straight down. Your throw ended when the ball left your hand.

Drawing a "force of motion" in the direction the object moves, or including a force the object exerts on something else (like the box pushing on the floor). Moving objects keep moving on their own, so no force is needed to "carry" the motion; and forces the box exerts belong on the floor's diagram, not the box's. Check: for every arrow, finish the sentence "___ pushes or pulls on the box".
